title: When an artery closes
narration: A blocked heart artery needs help fast. What happens next? In this example, a blood clot blocks a coronary artery. The heart muscle it supplies is suddenly short of oxygen. Emergency care can help restore blood flow.
visual_direction: Open on moving flow that stops at a clot. Within five seconds reveal the corresponding heart muscle territory before the title. No graphic injury.

title: Recognising a possible heart attack
narration: Warning signs can include chest pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or discomfort in the arm, back or jaw. The symptoms can differ from person to person. If a heart attack is suspected, call local emergency services immediately. Emergency responders can start assessment and coordinate hospital care.
visual_direction: Show a clothed anonymous person and a transition to emergency care. Use a short rotating pair of warning labels and keep emergency advice visible at the end.
on_screen_text: Suspect a heart attack? Call emergency services

title: Early assessment
narration: The emergency team considers the symptoms and uses an electrocardiogram, often called an ECG, to look at the heart’s electrical activity. A blood test called troponin can detect injury to the heart muscle. An ECG can sometimes identify a pattern that needs an immediate plan to reopen the artery.
visual_direction: Animate bedside leads on a clothed schematic and a distinct lab marker. Show a simulated tracing without labelling waveform details. Highlight two test names in sequence.

title: The emergency treatment path
narration: For a heart attack called STEMI, opening the artery quickly is a priority. When a team can perform emergency angioplasty promptly, it is generally the preferred way to restore flow. Emergency teams can use other pathways depending on access to treatment, test results, and the patient’s condition.
visual_direction: Show a simple emergency assessment-to-cath-lab transition. Keep alternate pathways neutral with no countdown, drug, procedural settings, or transfer instructions.

title: Finding the blockage
narration: In the catheter laboratory, the team uses contrast and moving X-rays to find the blockage. Here, contrast stops at the affected spot. The interventional cardiologist identifies the artery responsible for this heart attack and plans how to reopen it.
visual_direction: Keep the same coronary branch and clot from the opening. Show contrast stopping at the lesion in the simulated angiogram, then orient the viewer back to the cutaway.

title: Restoring flow
narration: The treatment is called percutaneous coronary intervention, or PCI. A thin guidewire can pass beyond the blockage. A balloon and, when appropriate, a stent are used to reopen and support the treated segment. The team then checks blood flow and looks for problems before the procedure ends.
visual_direction: Keep wire visible distal to the lesion while a mounted balloon-stent unit opens. Deflate and withdraw balloon while stent remains. Contrast returns downstream. Avoid depicting a clot being pushed into branches.

title: Recovery and prevention
narration: After the emergency treatment, the team monitors recovery and explains what the patient’s tests showed. Ongoing care can include medicines and cardiac rehabilitation. Some patients need a further assessment of other narrowed arteries. The team discusses the follow-up plan and what to do if symptoms return.
visual_direction: Move from a monitored bed to a simple follow-up and rehabilitation scene. Use light physical-activity silhouettes without patient-specific exercise prescription.
